title: Depression struggles, club dates and Joe Marcella
summary: Hard times in New York, club dates, Prima's band and the Marcella brothers; Dorr's unpaid wages.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: Plenty of us were. That was not unusual at all. There was a little guitar player from this town who's still here now by the name of Clayton Dyrd, I think it's D-U-E-R-R-R, D-E-U-R-R, known as Sunshine. A very fine guitar player. He played with the Joe Venuti Trio a while. And George Hartman from here. There were a whole bunch of people. I don't know how an upstate New York guy who was living and rooming with all these New Orleans fellas, but that's the way it happened. None of us was any too affluent. It was a matter sometimes of grabbing a one-spot job a week if you could grab it. The depression was on in its depths and money was scarce. Yet if you did grab a job or two, it would see you through just one or two spots. They called them club dates then. They didn't call them spot jobs. That's a New Orleans term I guess. They were strictly called club dates in New York. You get a club date. But of course they were all there hanging around waiting for the big chance, the chance to join up with a big road band or to make it big. A little band, Louis Prima, who must have been pretty young then, if I believe the age I saw a club printed for him recently in a magazine. Had a band in the old famous store, the first famous store. And he had, if I recall, practically Joe Marcella playing clarinet with him. And then later Joe Marcella moved over to the Hickory House with Winnie Anone playing clarinet. And there was a really fine clarinet player, Joe Marcella. Very good. Wasn't he originally from Buffalo, New York? No, I think he was from Chicago.
That's right. And there was another one from Buffalo, I think of it, named Hank DiMico, who also played around in quite a few bands and was rated very well. He was the Buffalo boy, Hank DiMico.
I don't know what's happened to him then.
Doesn't play anymore at all, I imagine.
I don't think so. He composed, maybe composes now. He had one hit, don't you remember? Don't cry at Joe? Oh yes, I remember.
I never connected that with Joe, my solid clarinet player.

I played with his brother Marty Marcella. So I played once in a band that was gotten together and managed by Ben Pollack, but it was under the name of Cheeple Marks, the first brothers. And in that band Marty Marcella was playing. George Wettling played drums in it. Quite a few other guys like that.
Back to Clayton Dorr, who was he playing with? Just spots? He didn't?

Oh, he played with some of the bands. Some of these bands that had a semi-name in those days are completely forgotten today. It was a band named Bob Sylvester that he played with. And when I met him, he was living with Bob Sylvester because he never had collected any money from him. And the only way he could collect any money from him was to live with him and deduct the lodging from what Sylvester owed him. And that was typical of the business in those days. And I guess the best he ever did was playing the stint with Joe Vanuti. Because Joe always had a name.
